items.name: Emergency toilet (bucket or folding)
items.need: When you are told not to flush, you still need somewhere safe to go that keeps waste contained inside a bag.
items.how_to_choose: When you are told not to flush, the toilet has to work without a sewer, and that means bags. A snap-on seat on a 5-gallon bucket is the cheapest route and is what the Portland-area twin-bucket method uses: one bucket for pee, one for poo. A folding toilet packs down to the size of a briefcase and is made for bag-and-gel kits. A separating toilet keeps pee and poo apart in one unit and controls smell best, at more than twenty times the price of a bucket. A flush-type camping toilet feels most like the one at home, but it needs water, and its 2.6 to 5.5 gallon tank has to be emptied into a working toilet or a dump station, which is the one thing you may not have.

qty.note: One toilet per household. For the twin-bucket method you need two 5-gallon buckets (one for pee, one for poo); one seat can be moved between them.

items.already_own: Your own toilet bowl can be lined with a heavy-duty bag if the bowl is intact and you empty the water first; King County's guidance describes lining a toilet bowl or a 5-gallon pail. Any clean 5- or 6-gallon bucket with a smooth rim also works as the base. Check that a bucket has no cracks and that a seat snaps on firmly before you rely on it.

safety_notes.text: Human poo can spread diseases such as cholera if it is not handled and stored safely, so it must be contained when toilets cannot be flushed.

Twin-bucket method: pee goes in one bucket and poo in a second bucket lined with a heavy-duty bag. Cover each poo with a handful of dry cover material, do not fill the bucket more than half full, and do not use an airtight lid on the bucket in use so the contents can dry.

The RDPO guide tells people to dilute pee and pour it on open ground such as a lawn, moving the spot each time. If you cannot get to open ground from your building, use bags with a gelling agent for pee as well.

Bleach is not part of the twin-bucket method. The RDPO guide's supply list is buckets, heavy-duty bags, dry cover material and hand-cleaning supplies; it does not call for bleach or other chemicals in the bucket.
Set up the toilet away from where food is prepared or eaten, and put a handwashing spot next to it.

Wash hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds after using or handling the toilet. If there is no soap and water, use hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol; it works less well on visibly dirty hands.
safety_notes.source_title: Guidelines for Personal Hygiene During an Emergency

safety_notes.text: A bucket holding even a few inches of liquid is a drowning hazard for babies and toddlers. If a small child lives with you or visits, keep every bucket that holds liquid lidded and behind a closed door, and never leave one where a small child can reach it.
safety_notes.source_title: In Home Danger: CPSC Warns of Children Drowning in Bathtubs, Bath Seats and Buckets (release 12-284, 2012)

items.name: Toilet bag kits with gelling agent
items.need: Bags that come with a gelling powder turn pee and poo into a gel, which matters when you cannot carry a pee bucket outside to empty it.
items.how_to_choose: Look at three things: how much liquid one bag can gel, whether there is a second zip-close bag to seal in smell during weeks of indoor storage, and the price per bag. Kits fit over a toilet bowl, a bucket or a folding toilet. They cost far more per day than a bucket with plain liners and cover material, so many households keep a small supply for the first days or for night use.

qty.note: 72 hours at home (3 days): one bag per use at 5 uses per person per day, which is 15 per person. Do not scale these up for two weeks: at two weeks switch to the bucket, liner and absorbent (X5-05, U5-19) and keep these kits for the first three days and for the bag. A child in diapers counts for diapers, not for toilet bags. Five uses a day is this site's planning figure; some makers say a bag can take more than one use, but the count here is one bag per use.

items.already_own: If you already have plain heavy-duty liners plus a gelling powder or dry cover material, you do not need kits. Unused camping 'wag bags' are fine if the packaging is still sealed and the powder inside is dry and loose.

safety_notes.text: Human poo can spread diseases such as cholera if it is not handled and stored safely, so it must be contained when toilets cannot be flushed.

Makers say used kits can go in the trash, but after a disaster do not put bags of human waste in regular garbage, recycling or yard-debris carts unless local authorities say so. Garbage is compacted and bags tear. Keep sealed bags until you are told how they will be collected, and never bury them.
Store sealed, double-bagged waste away from food, water, children, pets, flies and rats.
Wash hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds after handling waste bags. If there is no soap and water, use hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol.

items.name: Heavy-duty liner bags for the toilet or bucket
items.need: Plain strong bags line the toilet bowl or poo bucket and act as the second bag when you seal and store waste.
items.how_to_choose: Thickness is what matters, and it should be printed in mil. The RDPO guide asks for 13-gallon bags of 0.9 mil or thicker; Oregon State University Extension goes further and suggests 3 to 5 mil contractor-type bags. A practical setup is a 13-gallon bag as the liner and a thick contractor bag as the outer storage bag. Choose unscented bags and avoid anything sold as compostable or biodegradable, which is made to break down.

qty.note: Sized for two weeks at home, when you switch from bag kits to the bucket: one liner per person who uses the toilet for each day after the first three. Tie it off when the bucket is half full, or sooner. Tied liners then go, several at a time, into a thick contractor bag from the contractor bags item, which is the second bag. A child in diapers does not count. This is this site's estimate.

items.already_own: Kitchen bags you already have are good enough only if the box states 0.9 mil or more; many 13-gallon bags are thinner. If the box gives no thickness, use two bags as the liner and still double-bag for storage.

safety_notes.text: Line the poo bucket with a heavy-duty bag of 0.9 mil or thicker (13-gallon size is suggested). When the bucket is half full or less, tie the bag shut and put it inside a second bag.
Oregon State University Extension advises lining the poo bucket with a 13-gallon black bag 3 to 5 mil thick, then double-bagging full bags, sealing them and storing them away from food and water.

items.name: Cover and absorbent material
items.need: A dry cover material or gelling powder soaks up moisture, cuts smell and keeps flies off, which makes weeks of indoor bag storage bearable.
items.how_to_choose: For the twin-bucket method you want a dry, light, carbon-based material: the RDPO guide names sawdust, shredded paper and wood pellets, and avoids cedar. Wood pellets take the least room for what they do, because they swell to about three times their volume when wetted. If pee has to go in the bag too, a gelling powder is what stops it sloshing. Think about weight: a 40 lb bag is hard work on a staircase.

qty.note: Sized for two weeks at home, when you switch from bag kits to the bucket: enough for every person for each day after the first three. Each pick's size line shows how many person-days one package covers and the arithmetic behind it. A child in diapers does not count.

items.already_own: Shredded paper, pine pet bedding, peat moss or non-clumping pine cat litter you already have will do as cover material. It is good enough if it is dry, loose and not cedar. Keep a bagful beside the toilet with a scoop or cup.

safety_notes.text: After each use of the poo bucket, cover the surface with dry carbon material: the RDPO guide says about a handful, and Oregon State University Extension says about half a cup. Add more if pee gets into the poo bucket.
safety_notes.source_title: Survival Basics: Sanitation and Waste Management (EM 9334)

safety_notes.text: Wood pellets made for pellet stoves work as cover material: about 1 cup of water mixed with 2 cups of pellets makes about 6 cups of sawdust, so store extra water if you plan to use them.
Bleach is not required. The RDPO twin-bucket guide lists buckets, heavy-duty bags, dry cover material and hand-cleaning supplies, and does not call for bleach or other chemicals in the bucket.
Cat litter, fireplace ashes or sawdust can be put in the bottom of the bags lining a toilet bowl or pail.
Human poo can spread disease if it is not handled and stored safely; cover material reduces smell and flies but does not make the waste safe to touch.
Wash hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds after using the toilet or handling cover material near it. If there is no soap and water, use hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol.
safety_notes.source_title: Guidelines for Personal Hygiene During an Emergency

items.name: Lidded bin for storing sealed waste bags
items.need: Sealed bags of waste may have to wait weeks for collection, and they need a closed container that pets, flies and rats cannot get into.
items.how_to_choose: Pick steel where rats or mice are a possibility: outdoors, in a garage, on a balcony or in a shared utility room. The lid should grip or lock so it cannot be nosed open. Size the can to the people in your home: Oregon's planning figure is 5 gallons a person a week, so a 31-gallon can holds two weeks for three people and a 10-gallon can holds two weeks for one. A wheeled cart is far easier to move when it is full, but it is plastic. Smell control comes from tight double-bagging, not from the bin. Keep the bin out of direct sun and away from food and stored water.

qty.note: Ten gallons of can for each person at a two-week target (Oregon's planning figure is 5 gallons per person per week); one can for the household at a 3-day target. The count shown follows the size of the can you pick. This is an estimate of volume: bulky bags and diapers fill a can sooner.

items.already_own: A spare lidded garbage can that will not be emptied by haulers is what the RDPO guide suggests. A bucket with a screw-on gasket lid also works indoors. It is good enough if the lid stays on when the bin is knocked and nothing can chew through it where you keep it.

safety_notes.text: Store double-bagged poo away from food, water, children, pets, flies and rats. A separate garbage can that will not be picked up by haulers, or a spot in your home, is acceptable; well-sealed double bags should not smell.
Keep double-bagged waste in a secure place away from food and water, separate from other garbage, and listen for instructions from local waste haulers.
When services resume, do not put stored bags out with regular garbage unless local authorities say to. Follow emergency broadcasts for collection instructions and handle the bags with great care.
Double-bagged waste should be kept in a dedicated, secured garbage can protected from pets, flies and rats.

items.name: Contractor bags for household trash
items.need: When collection stops and the chute is closed, ordinary trash piles up inside your home, and thick bags keep it sealed and carryable.
items.how_to_choose: Look for a stated thickness of about 3 mil, which resists tearing on stairs and from broken glass after an earthquake. A full 42-gallon bag is heavy, so fill big bags part-way if you have stairs to carry them down, or pick a 33-gallon size, which also fits a standard 32-gallon can. Keep food waste tied in small bags inside the big one to hold down smell and pests, and keep these bags separate from any bags of human waste.

qty.note: One box per household is a sensible start; a 14-bag box covers a couple for about two weeks at one bag a day.

items.already_own: Any black bags you have marked 3 mil or 'contractor' are fine. Ordinary 30-gallon bags around 1 mil can stand in if you double them and keep sharp items wrapped.

safety_notes.text: Keep bags of human waste separate from ordinary garbage, and do not put human waste into the normal garbage.
safety_notes.source_title: Survival Basics: Sanitation and Waste Management (EM 9334)

safety_notes.text: Diapers go in regular garbage, not in the poo bucket, so household trash bags may hold them; tie them off well.
Ready.gov's basic kit list includes garbage bags and plastic ties for personal sanitation.
Wash hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds after handling trash. If there is no soap and water, use hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol.
